name: Dead Sea salt and mud treatments

lead: Dead Sea treatments use salts and mud from the very salty lake between Israel and Jordan. Products include mud masks, salt scrubs and mineral baths, sold for skin hydration and a refreshed look.
Clinical work focuses on psoriasis and joint pain. A 2018 trial in healthy women found a 30-minute mud application well tolerated, with short-lived moisturizing effects.

paras: People apply mud as a mask for around half an hour, use salt in baths or scrubs, or visit shore spas that combine bathing and sun exposure.

Single applications were tolerated in trials on healthy skin. Swallowing large amounts of Dead Sea water is toxic, and one review noted increased skin actinic damage in patients treated with sun exposure at the sea.

chain: Apply mud or salt to skin
angle.text: Mud masks and salt products deliver temporary moisturizing and an exfoliated feel; psoriasis patients may see lesion improvement in clinical settings.

lead: Dead Sea salt and mud treatments draw on a lake that is about 34 percent salt, roughly 9.6 times saltier than the ocean, with a mineral mix rich in magnesium, calcium and potassium and the highest bromide concentration of any water on earth.[1] The area has been a health resort destination for thousands of years.[1]

For appearance, the main use is topical: mud masks and salts used to leave skin feeling smoother and hydrated. A randomized trial of 75 healthy women found a single 30-minute application of three mud types produced short-lived moisturizing effects with no negative effect on barrier function, pH, redness or melanin.[2]

A systematic review found Dead Sea balneotherapy and climate beneficial for psoriasis and certain rheumatologic conditions, while noting no increase in skin cancers but more sun damage in treated patients.[3]

paras: Products include mud masks, salts, and bath treatments; cosmetic firms are interested in Dead Sea salts as skin-care ingredients.[1] Formulation studies examine thickeners and stability of mud masks.[4]

In a laser Doppler study, mud with different salt levels was tested for irritation on forearms.[5] The systematic review reported electrolyte-related toxicity only with ingestion of large amounts of the water.[3]

A systematic review reported benefit for psoriasis and rheumatologic disease.[3] A randomized trial found Dead Sea mud packs reduced chronic low back pain versus mineral-depleted packs.[6] A skin tolerance trial found temporary moisturizing and no barrier harm.[2]
